heading: Track k smallest with a heap
body: Merging k sorted lists naively takes O(Nk) — comparing k heads every time. Instead, use a **min-heap of size k** to always know which list has the next smallest element. Pop the min, append it, push its `.next` back. **O(N log k)** total.

heading: The (val, id, node) trick
body: Python's `heapq` compares tuples element-by-element. If two nodes have the same value, it tries to compare the nodes themselves → **TypeError**. Solution: store `(node.val, id(node), node)` so `id()` breaks ties without custom `__lt__`.

label: Core · Python
code:
from heapq import heappush, heappop

heap = [(head.val, id(head), head) for head in lists if head]
dummy = current = ListNode(0)

while heap:
    val, _, node = heappop(heap)
    current.next = node
    current = current.next
    if node.next:
        heappush(heap, (node.next.val, id(node.next), node.next))

return dummy.next

q: Why do we use `(node.val, id(node), node)` tuples instead of just `node` in the heap?
options: To avoid comparing ListNode objects when they have equal values
To make the heap operations faster
To save memory by storing references
To maintain the original order of the lists
explain: If two nodes have the same value, heapq would try to compare the ListNode objects directly → TypeError. id(node) breaks ties.
